title: Idle BIWTC ships may become floating hospitals for chars, haors
excerpt: Three idle BIWTC ships could become floating hospitals for haor, char and island areas, Prothom Alo reports. Staffing and costs are unsettled.
content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: The government is considering turning three of four idle passenger vessels owned by the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Corporation (BIWTC) into floating hospitals for people in haor, island and char areas, Prothom Alo reported on Friday (27 November).

The plan was discussed at a meeting of the shipping ministry, the health ministry and BIWTC at the Secretariat on 17 November, chaired by State Minister for Shipping Rajib Ahsan, according to the report. One vessel would become an eye hospital, one a maternal and child health hospital and one an orthopaedic surgery hospital, each with general physicians in an outpatient department. The fourth ship would be kept for government programmes.

The meeting agreed that the ships' basic design would stay the same, with one staircase turned into a ramp for patients. Accommodation, dining and sanitation for doctors and nurses and a hospital waste system would be arranged. Patients would pay a nominal fee, and the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) is to prepare a budget for equipment, Prothom Alo said.

The four ships have been lying idle at Badamtali Ghat near Sadarghat in Dhaka. MV Rupsha and MV Sugandha, bought from Western Marine Shipyard for Tk 68 crore, joined the fleet in February but are out of service because of few passengers and mechanical faults. MV Bangali and MV Modhumoti, bought for Tk 54 crore in 2014 and 2015, have also been idle for a long time. Officials blamed falling passenger numbers since the Padma Bridge opened in 2022.

"We can only provide the vessels; the physicians and nurses will have to come from the Ministry of Health, so much depends on their goodwill as well," Shipping Secretary Ataur Rahman Khan told Prothom Alo, adding that the three ships had not yet been chosen. Ministry sources said it was still unclear who would pay staff salaries, fuel and maintenance, what the conversion would cost and where the hospitals would operate.

Why it matters

People in chars, haors and islands travel long and costly distances for care, especially for childbirth, eye surgery and injuries. Devlens reported this week that shrinking rivers have cut off 550,000 char people in Kurigram and that richer groups now gain most from public hospital care. A floating service would need staff, referral links and a steady budget to work, which the plan does not yet have.

What to watch

  • The DGHS budget estimate for equipment and running costs.
  • Which three ships are chosen and which regions they will serve.
  • Whether the health ministry commits doctors and nurses, or seeks NGO or donor partners.
